newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Interest rate uncertainty hits dollar, stocks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Interest rate uncertainty hits dollar, stocks.

text.p: Uncertainty over interest rates dominated financial markets on Tuesday, sending the dollar skidding to five-month lows against the yen and causing sharp drops in European stocks.

Currency markets were hit by jitters that Japan might increase rates, making dollar-denominated assets less attractive to investors, while at the same time European equity investors fretted that U.S. rates were about to go up and sold stock.

The dollar fell by nearly three yen in early trade, weakened by reports that Japan's ruling Liberal Democratic Partly (LDP) committee was considering asking for higher discount rates from the Bank of Japan.

Currency traders -- unlike their equity colleagues-- also detected a shift of mood in Washington's commitment to a strong dollar ahead of a meeting of U.S. central bank policy-makers in the Federal Open Markets Committee (FOMC) later on Tuesday.

They cited comments by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin as evidence of Washington's change in tune. Rubin said the U.S. policy on the dollar remained unchanged -- but did not explicitly repeat his past support for a strong dollar.

The dollar, which recovered in early Europe slightly from its overnight low under 113 yen, has been spiralling downward since hitting a 56-month peak of 127.47 yen on May 1. Against the mark, it was down nearly two pfennigs

"People knew that Washington has been wanting a weak dollar against the yen in light of Japan's mushrooming surplus, but they had been unable to face up to the fact," said a chief trader at a major U.S. bank in Tokyo.

"Rubin's accumulated comments, the possibility the LDP will push for higher rates and the absence of any comments by the Japanese to halt the move...all helped the move," said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered.

The change of mood contrasted with trade on Monday where the dollar strengthened as investors bet on an increase in rates to come out of the FOMC. A decision was not expected before 1815 GMT, after European markets close.
Uncertainty over U.S. rates also loomed over European bourses. Frankfurt and Paris fell by over 1.5 percent as markets counted the extra cost of doing business.
Frankfurt suffered the most, with floor trade down 1.86 percent as the weaker dollar also hit exporting sectors. Many investors took up defensive positions ahead of the FOMC.
"Due to conflicting U.S. economic data, it is completely open as to if U.S. rates will be increased," a trader said.
In Paris, the blue-chip CAC-40 index fell 1.5 percent, with the market divided over no-change or a quarter percentage point rise in U.S. interest rates.

"We're coming up to a couple of key events -- the FOMC meeting, the French (parliamentary) election -- and the market's at record highs. It's normal to correct," one trader said. The CAC index rose 5.71 percent last week.

London slipped only 0.3 percent relieved that Wall Street had put in a strong performance overnight, where the Dow added nearly half a percent, but cautious ahead of the FOMC and fears of an imminent interest rate rise.
"It's all about the FOMC today," said one dealer "But it's a bit of relief that the (Wall) Street ended where it did, and for that reason we'll see a steady start," he added.
STOCK PRICES AT 0930 GMT
London's FTSE 100 was down 15.0 points at 4,630.2.
The Paris CAC-40 index was down 39.79 points at 2744.55.
Frankfurt's DAX index was down 70.63 points at 3534.09 .
CURRENCIES AT 0930 GMT
The dollar stood at 1.6939 marks and 113.60 yen compared with 1.7105 marks and 116.09 yen in late European trade on Monday.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed at $342.50 an ounce, compared to Monday's close in London of $341.25. Silver was at $4.72, up three cents.
